title: Exodus 23:14–19
context: Israel is to keep three annual feasts before the LORD: Unleavened Bread in the month Abib, recalling the exodus; Harvest, the first fruits of the field; and Ingathering at the year’s end. All males are to appear before the Lord GOD three times a year, and no one is to come empty-handed. Brief rules follow on sacrificial blood and fat, the best first fruits, and not boiling a young goat in its mother’s milk.

verses.text: “You shall observe a feast to me three times a year.
verses.arminianNotes: Three times a year Israel is to keep a feast to the LORD. Arminian readers see worship structured into the calendar as regular, joyful acts of remembering and responding to God’s goodness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God sets the terms of his own worship. The feasts are his appointment, not human invention, and they order Israel’s life around his works.

verses.text: You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib (for in it you came out of Egypt), and no one shall appear before me empty.
verses.arminianNotes: Unleavened Bread recalls the exodus in the month Abib. No one shall appear before me empty means worship includes giving back from what God has given. Arminian readers see grateful response at the heart of the feast.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the feast as a memorial of redemption and, with Passover, a type fulfilled in Christ, as 1 Corinthians 5:7–8 says. Coming with gifts acknowledges God as Redeemer and Provider.

verses.text: And the feast of harvest, the first fruits of your labors, which you sow in the field; and the feast of ingathering, at the end of the year, when you gather in your labors out of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: The feasts of Harvest and Ingathering, later called Weeks and Booths, celebrate the land’s first fruits and final yield. Arminian readers see thanksgiving for ordinary provision as part of faithful life with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence over seasons and harvest honored in worship. Many Christian readers note that Pentecost, the later name for the feast of Weeks, became the day the Spirit was poured out in Acts 2.

verses.text: Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: All males appear before the Lord GOD three times a year. Arminian readers note the gathering of the whole covenant people before their sovereign Lord, with representatives standing for each household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the title Lord GOD, sovereign Master and covenant LORD. Israel appears before its King in the assembly he summons.

verses.text: “You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leavened bread. The fat of my feast shall not remain all night until the morning.
verses.arminianNotes: Sacrificial blood is not to be offered with leaven, and the fat of the feast is not to remain until morning. Arminian readers see reverence for holy things and careful obedience in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God regulating the details of sacrifice. Many note that leaven often symbolizes corruption, though the precise reason for each rule is not explained in the text.

verses.text: You shall bring the first of the first fruits of your ground into the house of the LORD your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
verses.arminianNotes: The first of the first fruits belongs in the LORD’s house: God receives the best, not leftovers. Do not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk is repeated in 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21. Its reason is uncertain. Proposals include avoiding a pagan rite, showing humane respect for the bond of life, or keeping categories of life and death distinct. The text does not say.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress giving God the first and best. On the young goat they acknowledge uncertainty about its original purpose. Later Jewish tradition built its separation of meat and milk on it, while Christian interpreters have usually read it as one of Israel’s ceremonial laws.
